comment: plans/plan_xnapipeline_parity.md XNAPP-266 (§24): a difference between XNA's .xnb and CNA's is one of three things, and this file is the second of them. A case listed here differs for a reason that has been established and written down -- a deliberate divergence, or something this environment cannot settle. Everything not listed here and not identical is open, and fails the comparison. A decision whose case has since become identical also fails, so a reason cannot outlive what it explained. A decision may name the `paths` it explains, and then it explains only those: a case accepted for its compressed pixels stays open if its width changes, and a listed path that no longer differs fails the same way an obsolete decision does.

accepted.reason: Two conformant JPEG decoders disagree within an IDCT's tolerance. XNA decodes through D3DX and CNA through stb_image; the pixels differ by a few units and neither is wrong. Already recorded for the per-extension differential, which compares JPEG pixels within a tolerance rather than exactly (XNAPP-167).

A Radiance picture reaches XNA's TextureImporter as a PixelBitmapContent<Vector4> and its SpriteTextureProcessor converts those floats to Color; the canonical route decodes .hdr through the shared image decoder, whose RGBE-to-LDR conversion applies its own gamma. The XNA facade's own route answers the floats (RadianceHdrDecoder, XNAPP-167); it is the canonical Rgba8 route this case exercises. Open as a *design* question rather than a defect, and recorded so the choice is visible.

Block compression is lossy and every encoder chooses its endpoints differently. XNA compresses through D3DX; CNA through its own encoder. The dimensions, mip count, format and level sizes agree -- only the compressed bytes differ, which is what two DXT encoders always do.

The Xbox 360 stores a texture tiled, and XNA's pipeline tiles it for that target. CNA writes the untiled payload and refuses the platform by default for exactly this reason (--xnb-allow-unverified-xbox is needed to produce one at all). Lifting that refusal per type is XNAPP-252, and it needs hardware this machine does not have.

XNA converts a sound effect to XMA for the Xbox 360 -- format tag 0x6601, a big-endian XMA2WAVEFORMATEX, a quarter of the data. XMA is Microsoft's own codec with no public specification and no licensable encoder, so CNA answers the Windows PCM payload instead. Measured and recorded at the processor level too (soundeffectprofile/*, XNAPP-021); .wav's xbox360 row reads UNSUPPORTED.

Everything in this effect that CNA decides is now XNA's, byte for byte, including the container header: the pair of dwords per pass that records which device state the pass disturbs and which sampler registers it binds (XNAPP-191). What is left, over all seventeen effect cases, is 195 bytes inside the compiler's own version string and 54 bytes of padding -- and nothing else at all. XNA's pipeline compiles in-process through d3dx9 and stamps 'Microsoft (R) HLSL Shader Compiler 9.26.952.2844' into each shader blob; the June 2010 SDK's fxc.exe, which is the newest legacy compiler that can write an fx_2_0 container, stamps 9.29.952.3111. The padding is the other side of the same coin: d3dx9 leaves the bytes after each aligned string as whatever was in its heap ('but', 'st_', fragments of other names), where fxc zeroes them. Neither is reproducible without running Microsoft's own in-process compiler, and the second should not be reproduced at all.

CNA has no canonical .xml route. Of the 1466 .xml assets in the public sample corpus, almost all declare game-defined types, which only a game's own pipeline assembly can build (XNAPP-260); a built-in route could cover the handful the framework itself defines and would be XNB-only. The decision to build that subset has not been taken.

Two rasterizers disagree about a glyph's ink by a pixel. XNA draws through GDI+ and CNA through FreeType, and over the 95 glyphs of this font 40 boxes are identical, 50 are one pixel wider, four are two wider and one is a pixel wider and taller -- never narrower. Everything derived from a glyph's box follows it: its rectangle in the sheet, the cropping rectangle's width, and the compressed pixels. The metrics that decide where text lands do not: the ABC widths are identical for all 95 characters, the cropping origin for 94 of them, and the line spacing exactly (plans/plan_xnapipeline_parity.md XNAPP-182). The cropping rectangle's height is XNA's own and is between one and five pixels more than its line spacing, by an amount no metric in the face predicts: Courier New and Liberation Mono are metrically identical and answer 41 at size 24, where Arial -- whose line height is larger -- answers 40. Eleven builds over four faces were measured and no rule fits them, so CNA writes the line spacing itself. SpriteFont.MeasureString() reports the taller of that and the tallest glyph, so a measured string is up to five pixels shorter here. The space's cropping rectangle is XNA's degenerate one: it has no ink, and XNA's cropper answers a cell at an offset past the bottom of the line (6, 35 in a 24-pixel cell) where CNA answers the origin. Nothing draws it either way.
